paragraphs.text: Truly new and very great is the theater of piety that the chorus of the three youths has assembled. In Babylon they fought the good fight, but throughout the whole world they make the wonder of their martyrdom ring out. For the glory of the saints is not confined to a place, nor is the memory of the righteous bounded by time: "For the righteous will be held in everlasting remembrance." So although the martyrdom was completed in very ancient times, the feat of their endurance is sung for all ages. We know the events through the readings, we know the story through memory, and through the word, as in a picture, we see both the lawlessness of the tyrant and the confession of the saints. We see the furnace blazing with fire and flaring back against the tyrant's rage, and showing the martyrs' confession unquenched by the threat of fire. But why not go back to the beginning and tell the contests of these truly God-loving and thrice-blessed men? Nebuchadnezzar the king, or rather the tyrant (for that is the fitting name for a lawless man), ruled over Babylonia. He was barbarous in soul and savage in character. Drunk with great injustice, wealth and impiety, he forgot his own nature. He did not even think of himself as a man, but expected to be worshiped as a god. His overweening arrogance was fed both by his own inborn madness and by the long-suffering of God, who patiently bears with the impious and allows all things to happen for the training of the pious. This lawless man made a golden image, that is, a golden statue, and he compelled those who were made in the image of God to worship the image that he had made. Sparing no expense, he gave it a height of sixty cubits and a breadth of six cubits. He made the statue well proportioned and graceful, so that falsehood might overpower the truth and win the day, either by the size of the statue or by the beauty of its design. So the craftsmanship gleamed, the gold shone, the herald shouted, the tyrant threatened, the furnace blazed. On top of all this, the so-called instruments of music whipped the foolish into a terrible frenzy of godlessness, and the spectacle before their eyes robbed all who watched of their understanding. But the command of impiety was not going to overcome the saints as well. Practically everyone was being swept over the cliff of idolatry, as if by a torrent, by the violent current of deceit. But these three noble young men faithfully planted themselves on piety as on a rock, and were not carried off by the current of injustice. For it was fitting for them to say: "If the Lord had not been among us, they would have swallowed us alive. When their wrath was kindled against us, the water would have drowned us. Our soul passed through a torrent; our soul would have passed through the overwhelming water." But they were neither drowned by the current nor caught in the snares. Running well toward piety and using the lofty wing of faith, they were kept safe, as the author of Proverbs says: "Like a gazelle from the snares, and like a bird from the trap." Seeing the devil's nets spread out, as it were, over all humanity, they repeated the pious words of the psalmist: "Sinners shall fall into their own net." The three captives did not consider their own smallness, though so many were pressing them hard. They knew very well that even the smallest spark of piety is enough to burn up and destroy all impiety. That is why, though they were only three, they strengthened one another and held tightly together. For they knew that "narrow and hard is the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it." They remembered the patriarch Abraham. He was the only worshiper of God in all the earth, yet he did not follow the crowd of the impious, but the prize of piety and righteousness was his law. So it was fitting that from him, as from a good root, these fruits of piety should spring. For from him came the patriarchs, Moses the lawgiver, the prophets and all who spoke of God. Above all, from him came that saving and immortal flower of righteousness, the Savior's taking on of human nature. From that same line came these three youths, and they did not betray their noble birth. They remembered also Lot, who lived as a stranger in Sodom but kept himself far removed from its ways. They kept in mind Joseph too, who alone in Egypt held fast to chastity and was a school of piety. So these youths, too, hemmed in among so many tens of thousands, looked at the many and reflected that "wide and spacious is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who find it." Then, looking again at themselves and at the furnace, they remembered the words of Wisdom somewhere: "As gold is tested in a furnace, so God chooses hearts." Therefore the trumpet sounding its martial strain did not frighten them. The lyre charming the ear did not slacken the strings of their piety. Nor did all the rest of the musical ensemble break up the fair and harmonious music of their piety. Instead, against that fair harmony they set their fair confession. When that evil-minded and impious tyrant heard that Hananiah and his companions were disobeying the command of lawlessness, his soul swelled with diabolical pride. Putting on, so to speak, the very face of the prince of evil, he summoned them and said: "Is it true, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, that you do not serve my gods and do not worship the golden image that I have set up?" He thought piety was a mere show, and asked whether those who professed piety really dared to defy royal commands. But he was to learn from experience itself that the men of God not only spit upon the tyrant's threats, but by the power of piety will also trample down the full force of the fire itself. "Now then, as soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, the pipe and the lyre, the sambuca, the harp, the symphonia and every kind of music, fall down and worship the golden image that I have set up."

He described the worship of demons well: "Fall down and worship." Those who worship demons cannot help falling into ruin and falling away from the truth. "But if you do not worship," he says, "you shall be thrown that very hour into the furnace of burning fire." Surely if it is a furnace, there is obviously fire; and if there is fire, obviously it is burning. But he enlarges and swells the threat in order to bend the resolve of piety: "You shall be thrown that very hour into the furnace of burning fire." Up to this point his arrogance is bearable. But see what he adds next: "And who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?" Here is another Pharaoh. For Pharaoh too said to Moses: "Who is God, that I should obey him?" "I do not know the Lord," says the impious man, "and I will not let the people go." O the great arrogance of human beings! O the great long-suffering of God! A man speaks, and God endures it. The clay talks, and the Potter is patient. A tongue of flesh speaks, and the Master of the bodiless angels has compassion, he "who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire." This is the right moment to recall the words of Isaiah: "Why is earth and ashes so arrogant?" Do you want to marvel at God's long-suffering? Think about an insult done to you, and how unbearable you have thought it to be. Someone is often insulted by a slave, and at once he holds up his own status as a free man against the insult. He demands justice for the outrage and punishes the offender with a death that no plea can avert. Again, someone holds office in the affairs of this world and is insulted by a lowly private person. At once, stung by the insult, he hurries to take revenge. He does not consider our common nature and the equal dignity of all, but looks to the rank that surrounds him. Strip that rank away, and you can see the single equality of our race: we were all formed from earth, and we are all dissolved into earth. There is one way into life, and the departure is the same for all. "You were formed from clay," it says, "just as I was." Yet the clay demands such superiority over its equals. God, however, surpasses all things both by nature and by right, and he is as much higher than they are as a maker must be thought loftier than the things he has made. Yet when he is blasphemed and scorned by the ungrateful, he is not provoked, for he is beyond passion. But a little later he punishes those who persist in their folly, because he is a judge of truth and a judge who cannot be swayed. So that all sinners may not be destroyed at once, he postpones punishment and offers forbearance, to draw them to repentance. But let us return to our subject. A man clothed in flesh dared to say: "Who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?" When the thrice-blessed youths heard this, they did not fly into a rage at the blasphemy, for they too had been raised on God's long-suffering. Instead they took up the voice of faith against the words of unbelief and answered the tyrant. They undid lawlessness by law and overcame the threat of injustice by the freedom of righteousness, saying: "Be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods and do not worship the golden image that you have set up." Stop your folly, man! Be ashamed of this outrageous worship of an image. If you set up the image, how can you worship what you made? Who ought to be the maker of whom: men the makers of God, or God the maker of men? If they were really gods, the dignity of creating would belong to them. But as we have often said before, if human beings did not have craftsmanship, the Greeks would have no gods. Or rather, let us notice this too: if idols had any feeling, they ought to worship the men who make them. For it is a law of nature that the thing made worships its maker, not that the craftsman bows down to his own handiwork. "Therefore we, who were raised in piety, follow the divine law. We do not serve your gods and do not worship the golden image that you have set up. But there is a God in heaven who will deliver us out of your hands." Then, so that they would not seem either to be testing God or to be bold in the face of the fire only because they hoped to be rescued, they at once add: "But if not." That is: even if he does not rescue us but allows our bodies to be burned by the fire, not even then will we abandon piety. For we do not revere God for wages, but with gratitude we confess the truth. When the tyrant heard this profession of faith, he burned hotter still and ordered the furnace to be heated seven times over. For the most precious silver had to be refined seven times: "The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tried by fire, tested in the earth, refined seven times." Therefore the furnace was heated seven times over, so that the saints might be purified seven times over. That the men of God are called silver, remember Wisdom saying: "The tongue of the righteous is refined silver." Hear also the prophet Jeremiah speaking about those who are rejected for lack of piety: "Call them rejected silver, for God has rejected them." If the imperfect are rejected silver, then clearly those who have been perfected are the most precious silver. For the hotter the furnace was heated, the more brightly their longing for martyrdom shone. These three holy youths entered with faith and trod down the flame, breathing a light and dewy air in the very midst of the fire's fury. For he who makes and transforms all things blunted the heat of the fire and cut short its power to burn, and the miracle proved the truth of that hymn: "The voice of the Lord who divides the flame of fire." The fire lay quietly inside as if asleep, while the holy youths danced. They were all but enjoying the promise that God makes through the prophet Isaiah to every soul full of piety and faith: "Even if you pass through fire, I am with you, and the flame shall not burn you." One could see the promise being carried out in deeds. For the fire did not touch the limbs of the saints. It did not burn their eyes, which looked rightly toward piety and had come to know the Maker of the world through the beautiful order of visible things. It did not harm their ears, which were filled with the divine law. It did not come near their mouths or touch their lips, but shrank back in reverence before their tongues, which sang and composed hymns. Each of the saints' limbs had its own safeguard: their hands, being stretched out in prayer and giving alms; their breasts, the power of piety dwelling within; their bellies and the parts below, the practice of chastity; their feet, the race of virtue. But why should I linger over every detail? The fire did not even dare to touch their hair, because piety covered it more than their turbans did. It even spared their clothing, out of respect for the saints' decency. What then? After this God commands the fire to seize the Chaldeans. They might have thought it was magic that had dimmed the fire's power, and so have belittled the glory of the martyrs and slandered the miracle of truth. To prevent this, those inside remained at peace while the fire outside fed on the Chaldeans. In this way it convinced the onlookers beyond doubt that in the case of the saints it had not forgotten its own nature, but had honored their piety, just as the lions in the den had done with Daniel. And so from then on the thrice-blessed youths formed a truly angelic choir and sang hymns to God. They gathered all creation, both what is above the world and what is seen with the eyes, into a single chorus of praise.

We must also not leave this question unexamined: why did they not name the whole creation all at once, instead of setting out the created world part by part? As far as the truth is concerned, it would have been enough to say: "Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord." But this great theater of piety was being assembled in the land of the impious, and so the Babylonians had to be taught which things are creatures and who is the Maker of all. They begin with the angels and end with human beings. Angels were thought to be gods. Among the Greeks there is even a story that says: "These gods whom we worship are angels of the great God." So, to teach the foolish that the angels belong not among those who are worshiped but among those who worship, they cry out: "Bless the Lord, you angels of the Lord." The sun and moon and the whole chorus of the stars were worshiped. That is why they also bring these into the worship of their hymns: "Bless the Lord, sun and moon; bless the Lord, stars of heaven." Then after these: "Every shower and dew, bless the Lord." It would be good to consider what is meant by "every shower and dew, and all the winds." Droughts often occur, and violent winds out of season. Those who invent falsehoods and delight in vanity always like to blame everything on some kind of matter and on the evil of disorder. They do not know that nothing is without a master or happens in vain, but that God governs all these things, both to teach human beings and to turn them away from impiety. For the good order of created things usually proclaims their Creator, while their disorder calls to account those who worship created things. If rain or wind were something divine and worthy of worship, they would not be disorderly, for the divine admits no disorder. That is why they say: "Every shower and dew and all the winds, bless the Lord." Rains and winds were also worshiped, the rains as nourishers of the earth's fruits and the winds as their cultivators. The earth was worshiped too, and its fruits were assigned to various demons: they called the vine the gift of Dionysus, the olive the gift of Athena, and other fruits the gifts of other gods. To guard against this, the same word of truth says: "Bless the Lord, all things that grow on the earth." For he is the Creator and Master of all that has grown and still grows. After this come mountains and hills. Are the mountains and hills then something apart from the earth? Not at all. But since the foul shrines of the demons were built on the hills, and statues were worshiped there, he says: "Bless the Lord, mountains and hills." After mentioning the hills, he also mentions springs, rivers and the sea. For these too were made into gods: they called the springs Nymphs and the sea Poseidon, and spoke of Sirens and Nereids. That rivers too were worshiped is shown by what is done in Egypt to this day. They sacrificed to the rising of the Nile, not marveling at God in its nature, but serving the water itself as a god. That is why they call the rivers, the springs and the sea into the hymn. Then come the birds of heaven and the cattle, for these too were not exempt from being made into gods. The eagle was worshiped, and the hawk. The Egyptians honored wild beasts and cattle with the name of gods. The error was so strong that they even named cities after the animals they worshiped, and they have cities named after dogs, sheep, wolves and lions. After all these, the human race is finally brought forward: "Bless the Lord, you sons of men." The human race is placed last, not because of its rank, but because of the order of creation. "Bless the Lord, Israel." He brings forward the race that was set apart from all the people on earth, and he lays out the many ranks within that nation at that time. He brings forward the priests of the Lord to put to shame the priests of the falsely named gods. Then he says: "Servants of the Lord." Then, so that those who have departed this life would not seem to be strangers to this choir, they count them among the living before God, saying: "Bless the Lord, spirits and souls of the righteous." Then: "Holy and humble of heart, bless the Lord." Why does he mention the holy and the humble? To show that God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble. He burned up the arrogant outside the furnace, and preserved the holy and humble in the midst of the fire. That is why the fire, too, joined the saints in their dance, for along with everything else it was commanded to praise the Creator: "Bless the Lord, fire and heat." This was so that the Babylonian magi, who honor fire, might learn that fire is not among those who are worshiped, but among those who worship. But let us come to the last verse and end our sermon. "Bless the Lord," it says, "Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael." After so many ranks had been listed, what need was there to add themselves by name at the end? Were they not blessing God among the sons of Israel? Were they not counted among the servants of the Lord when they said, "Bless the Lord, servants of the Lord"? Or when they said, "holy and humble of heart," were they not counted among the holy? What then does this added line mean: "Bless the Lord, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael"? The miracle was extraordinary and beyond human nature, for they entered the furnace in the body and trod it down. Some of those in error, struck by the strangeness of the miracle, might dare to call them gods and worship those who had overcome the fire, which would seem more reasonable than worshiping the fire itself. To keep the onlookers from falling into such an error, they declare that they are servants and confess that they themselves worship, saying: "Bless the Lord, Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael." It is said that this is also why God did not allow Daniel to be taken into this martyrdom. He had interpreted the king's dream, and the king himself had worshiped him as a god, and he had been called Belteshazzar after the name of the god of the Persians. So, to keep anyone from thinking that the fire's power had ceased because of the name Belteshazzar that he bore, God arranged for Daniel not to be brought forward, so that the miracle of piety might remain pure. But enough of this.

Through the prayers and intercessions of the martyrs, may we take up the same zeal, be counted worthy of the same praise and obtain the same kingdom, by the grace and loving-kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.
